system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling dizzy and really weak. My stomach and back hurt more than usual, and I’ve had diarrhea all day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were just discharged a few days ago for confusion and a possible infection. How have you been since then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt okay at first, but yesterday I started feeling dizzy. My blood pressure was going up and down at home. And I’ve been confused again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sister mentioned you seemed like your usual self. Can you tell me what the confusion feels like?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I repeat myself, I can’t focus, and I forget simple things. It comes and goes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the diarrhea—what does it look like?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s watery, and at the end it looks black. But it’s not tarry or bloody. I stopped taking my lactulose because I’ve had so many bowel movements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We tested your stool and it’s not showing signs of a C. diff infection. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection? Why am I so sick?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver disease can cause these symptoms. Your belly is distended, which may be from fluid buildup. That could be making your pain worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been eating much—just popsicles and crackers. I was scared to eat real food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. We’re going to get you back on your regular diet. You also had an ultrasound today. It shows your liver is enlarged, which we expected, but no blockages or gallstones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the pain from my liver?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely, yes. The pain around your lower belly and back could be from the stretching of the liver capsule and the fluid pressing on things. We don’t think it’s an infection in your belly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are improving. Your white blood cell count has gone down, and you haven’t had any diarrhea since yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel a little better. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re restarting your diuretics—spironolactone and furosemide—because your fluid levels are stable. We’re also lowering your lactulose dose to 15 mL three times a day to avoid too many bowel movements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll keep taking your citalopram, oxazepam, and rifaximin. No changes there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you keep feeling this way, we can discharge you today. You’ll need to follow up with your primary doctor in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What should I watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If the diarrhea comes back, or if you feel more confused, dizzy, or have fever, you should come back. Also, keep eating regular meals and drinking fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. Your discharge papers are ready. You’re doing well, and we’re confident you can recover at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll make sure to take my meds and eat better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And call your doctor if anything changes. You have an appointment next week?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I do. I’ll go.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old woman with Child's class B alcoholic cirrhosis, portal hypertension, ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy was admitted for dizziness, diarrhea, and acute worsening of chronic abdominal and back pain. She had been recently discharged after treatment for hepatic encephalopathy and a suspected UTI. On admission, she reported watery diarrhea with black residue at the end, though stool tested negative for C. difficile. Her mental status was variable but consistent with baseline encephalopathy. Labs showed elevated WBC that improved by discharge. Imaging revealed cirrhosis with trace ascites and no acute pathology. Diuretics were held initially due to diarrhea but restarted before discharge. Symptoms resolved during the hospital stay, and she was discharged home with follow-up planned. Pending stool and blood cultures remained unresolved at discharge.
